Hi [~accountid:6169660ebfa2c1006b56c18f],

Please find below some further advice regarding the possibility of suspending an account following multiple fines.

Article 3.2.5 of the T&Cs allows for Bolt to suspend or deactivate an account if the user breaches the Terms and Conditions in accordance with Article 8.3. 

Additionally, Article 5.8 provides for the possibility to suspend the account if there are outstanding payments owed to Bolt past the due date. However, the account will be unsuspended once the outstanding payments have been settled by the user. 

As such, our T&Cs enables the suspension of an account for breach of the rules of conduct subject to a prior communication.

*Where?* {color:#006644}Restaurant App{color}

*Function:* [https://clarity.microsoft.com/mobile-apps|https://clarity.microsoft.com/mobile-apps|smart-link]  – understanding how Users interact with features, instant heat-maps, understanding how specific customer behaves (phone model, operating system, custom attributes).

Purpose of the personal data processing: analyze the activity and characteristics of app and users, e.g. capturing data about mouse movement and performance – 🔴  {color:#bf2600}*essentially Restaurant app impression tracking for analytics purposes?*{color}

*Personal Data:* Courier phone number + name, Eater partial name + phone number + address (in case of Restaurant own delivery), Order data

*Retention duration:* 24 hours after the order submission

*T&Cs:* [https://clarity.microsoft.com/terms|https://clarity.microsoft.com/terms|smart-link] 

*Data Protection Clause 4*

🔴 4.4.(c).i: C-C (independent controllers)

* :yellow_circle:  Microsoft may collect statistical data about your use of the Clarity Service
* 🔴  You will disclose in your privacy notice the fact that Microsoft collects or receives Personal Data from you to provide Microsoft Advertising, and provide a link to the Microsoft Privacy Statements:  https://privacy.microsoft.com/en-us/privacystatement 
* 🔴 Microsoft may use the Personal Data it collects in connection with the Offering for any purpose in accordance with the Microsoft Privacy Statement, including to provide the Offering; improve Microsoft’s products and services, including reporting and performance analysis; and create user profiles for purposes that include advertising. Microsoft may also use nonpersonal data it collects in connection with the Offering to provide and improve Microsoft’s products and services.



*Privacy Analysis (my thoughts)*

* {color:#006644}*The main factor decreasing the privacy risk:*{color} We’re tracking *restaurant app* (how Restaurant or Store is using the app – the provider, not data subject i.e. Courier / Eater
* The main red flags are that from the “Offering” (service description), {color:#bf2600}*the relationship should be C-P*{color} and Microsoft Clarity should be more restrained in their processing activities. The product is {color:#bf2600}*“free”*{color}, meaning there’s little room for negotiation – {color:#bf2600}*higher risk of Microsoft Clarity using the Personal Data “for any purpose.. including create User profiles that include advertising”*{color}{color:#bf2600} {color}→ Might be tricky given the fact that we don’t have PN for Merchants (in the backlog) + there’s a requirement to provide a link to Microsoft’s PN. 
* The data flow is unclear – Will Microsoft see all actins taken on app, including the personal data of Eaters and Couriers? If yes, coupled by the previous paragraph, this poses privacy risks. Given that they’re not a processor and we cannot instruct them with how to process the data they’ll have access to 
* *Final unclarity, and perhaps to start with:* why are we opting for Microsoft Clarity? Can’t we use Mixpanel and tools we already have?

*Intelligent Recommendations and Defaulting* for Expense Items uses the following information from the scanned receipts and expense submitter for Expense Item predictions:

* Merchant Name
* Currency Code
* Receipt Amount
* Receipt Date
* Expense Payee

For the combination of input fields, Workday recommends up to 5 most likely Expense Items. In scenarios where the Machine Learning (ML) model is +confident+, the value of the field is defaulted with the top Expense Item recommendation.

Intelligent Recommendations and Defaulting for Expense Items uses tenant-specific models that are trained on customer contributed data. The customer contributed data might include historical data of expense report lines that are approved and created from an OCR scanned receipt. 

Recommendations won’t be shown in Workday with poor prediction accuracy.

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

Some stats to evaluate how much we over refund in such a way:

{noformat}select
	scre.currency,
	COUNT(*) as no_of_over_refunds,
	SUM(scre.amount) as refunded_sum,
	SUM(scre.amount_eur) as refunded_eur,
	SUM(CAST(json_extract_scalar(scre.action_payload, '$.payload.compensation.amount') as double)) as requested_sum,
	SUM(
		CAST(json_extract_scalar(scre.action_payload, '$.payload.compensation.amount') as double) / (scre.amount / scre.amount_eur)
	) as requested_sum_eur,
	SUM(
		scre.amount - CAST(json_extract_scalar(scre.action_payload, '$.payload.compensation.amount') as double)
	) as could_save, 
	SUM(
		scre.amount_eur -
		CAST(json_extract_scalar(scre.action_payload, '$.payload.compensation.amount') as double) / (scre.amount / scre.amount_eur)
	) as could_save_eur,
	AVG(
		scre.amount -
		CAST(json_extract_scalar(scre.action_payload, '$.payload.compensation.amount') as double)
	) as avg_over_refunded_per_case
from customer_support.support_case_refund_executed scre
join core_models.dim_city c on scre.city_id = c.city_id
where
	scre.action_type = 'ridehailing_discount_campaign'
	and scre.created between DATE('2024-12-01') and DATE('2025-01-01')
	and json_extract_scalar(scre.action_payload, '$.payload.compensation.type') = 'partial_refund'
	and CAST(json_extract_scalar(scre.action_payload, '$.payload.compensation.amount') as double) < scre.amount
group by 1
limit 100;{noformat}

{quote}The invoice was not generated as the driver did not owe any commission to Bolt or he had more compensation than owed commission.{quote}

Hello Igor! So sorry for not replying to this, I must have missed the notification. I am checking this now and will get back to you ASAP 🙂

+*FEATURE ANALYSIS*+

* Risk Profile = {color:#ff5630}*High*{color}
** Categories of data are not particularly controversial, nor is the purpose (i.e., to increase likelihood of acceptance of trips).
*** For good measure, we should ensure a PPRA is conducted, as I understand that one has not.
** However, the following factors raise the risk profile:
*** We are matching various datasets to fulfil this purpose. Data processing here will be on a large scale, using a novel algorithm, and involve a lot of geolocation data.
*** At present, the data processing could be regarded as ‘invisible’.
*** The processing would be fully automated, without feasible scope for human intervention.
*** The processing ultimately affects the price that will be paid to drivers. This creates a risk of  drivers questioning why some are paid more than others for apparently similar conditions. Over a prolonged period, this could also affect driver earnings.
*** The regulators (ICO / AKI) and worker activist groups (WIE / Taxiunionen) are currently very interested in how driver fees are calculated. This would further complicate the picture.
** As such, we should conduct a DPIA.
* Categories of personal data (for good measure, we should confirm this):
** Driver data:
*** Type of order (e.g. business or personal trip)
*** Ride category (e.g. Bolt, comfort, premium, pets, etc)
*** Price estimation and adjustments (including surge multipliers and promo discounts)
*** Actual and estimated trip distance and duration
*** Pick-up and drop-off GPS location
*** Acceptance rate
*** Acceptance / rejection of a specific order
*** Driver ID / basic profile information
*** Availability status
** Rider data:
*** Order request details (e.g., time, location, and ride category)
*** Geolocation data (e.g., pickup and drop-off coordinates
*** Passenger ID / basic profile information
** Data generated via the model:
*** Order try elasticity
* Legal basis here would be legitimate interest.
** As such, we should conduct a LIA.
** This should be covered in the current draft of the driver [privacy notice|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TDCY5_gJrlcpDLHKT0x9NMP4IRp1BmL0/edit] (at present, legitimate interest seems to be missing from the relevant row).
* Article 22:
** This would count as solely automated decision-making.
** Core question is whether this _significantly_ affects drivers. We could argue that it does not (as only increases fare for certain drivers by 10%, although {color:#ff5630}*we need to be careful - could be perceived as risk of discrimination / affect an individual’s earnings*{color}).
** If this was caught by A22, we could not feasibly rely on consent nor human review.
* Transparency:
** Risk of driver awareness (it may not be clear to drivers why their fare has been increased for certain trips). Means of mitigating this is through clear distinction in UI.
** This should be covered in the current draft of the driver [privacy notice|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TDCY5_gJrlcpDLHKT0x9NMP4IRp1BmL0/edit] (at present, the ‘To calculate prices’ row does not sufficiently cover this).
* Back-end processing / DSRRs:
** We need to ensure that this is somehow reflected in the data we are providing in response to DSARs (i.e., order history).

+*OVERLAP WITH ICO INVESTIGATION*+

* _5. Please identify all the data categories/factors/rate elements which might influence the calculation of Estimated Journey Fees._
** Our position here should be is that it was true at that time.
* _6. Please explain how each of the data categories/factors/rate elements identified in response to question 5 influence the calculation of Estimated Journey Fees._
** Our position here should be is that it was true at that time.
* _7. Please confirm whether the calculation of Estimated Journey Fees is a fully automated process with no human involvement. If there is any human involvement, please describe the nature of that human involvement._
** DC will not affect this.
** Of course if it automated. Our position is it does not produce a similarly significant effect (but need to be careful).
* _8. What algorithmic technique does Bolt use to calculate Estimated Journey Fees (e.g. decision tree, random forest, rule/decision lists and sets)?_
** Our position here should be is that it was true at that time.
* _10. Please provide a complete list of reasons for why a Journey Fee might differ from the corresponding Estimated Journey Fee._
** Our position here should be is that it was true at that time.
* _11. Are drivers provided with reasons for why a particular Journey Fee differs from the Estimated Journey Fee which was indicated to them?_
** Given sensitivity, I would introduce more transparency here.
* _12. Please confirm whether the calculation of Journey Fees is a fully automated process with no human involvement. If there is any human involvement, please describe the nature of that human involvement._
** DC will not affect this.
** Of course if it automated. Our position is it does not produce a similarly significant effect (but need to be careful).

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Steps for Privacy:
** Conduct a PPRA.
** Conduct a LIA.
** Conduct a DPIA.
** Update the current draft of the driver privacy notice.
* Steps for Stakeholders:
** Ask stakeholders for a full list of personal data being processed here, as well as more info on the algorithm.
** Flag to stakeholders that if we launch this, drivers will be able to see it (through DSARs) and so will WIE / ICO (as may well be subject to disclosure).
*** Ask stakeholders how DC will be explained to drivers. Will there by guidance materials? Something in the UI?
** Ensure that DC is covered in DSAR responses.
** Ask stakeholders whether drivers will similarly be able to challenge the revised fee here.

Thanks for your patience while waiting for the reply. 

We definitely shouldn’t overlook any queries. Ideally, drivers should be able to skip through Alfred and get the support they need from a CS agent. New drivers, especially during market launches, have different needs compared to already established markets, and we’re mindful of that. 

The Central OPS team is already working on onboarding/guidance that will help explain the basics of the app and introduce all the features and settings to drivers who have no experience with the platform. If you notice any recurring issues, including this one, you can reach out to Oliver Martyn Vahar, who’s leading this project, to see if they’re planning to address it.

For existing drivers, CXA is conducting an analysis of what they're missing and what adds friction to our support. This will help us collaborate with other teams as well, and improve the support experience based on clear data.

In Support Solutions, we have limited ability to influence how the AI works. Even when our FAQs provide the solution, we’ve seen cases where Alfred focuses on just one detail and doesn’t offer other helpful info from the same article. What we can do is add labels to articles so that cases are directed straight to the support team, but this isn’t possible for content that doesn’t exist. It’s a great point you’ve raised, especially since the AI doesn’t recognise when it’s providing inaccurate info. If you’d like to take this concern further, it would be best to reach out to the team responsible for the AI logic in #[dev-support-automation-support|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C064FCFAT0S].

Right now, we’re juggling many projects, so we have to prioritise where we focus our time. Our top priority has always been to streamline our internal processes and work on articles that have the biggest impact on reducing CS volumes.

Thank you for your understanding, and have a nice day! ☀️

Hey [~accountid:621f66fc4160640069c66ff9] 🙂 

The key reason we *do not* discuss financial transactions over the phone is due to *security and data protection risks*. We need to ensure that financial-related actions (such as refunds, payouts, or billing disputes) are handled *securely* and with proper verification, which is not always possible over a phone call.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. *What agents can say to callers instead of “we’re not allowed”:*
{panel}

* "For security reasons, we only process financial transactions through our verified support channels where we can properly authenticate your request."
* "To protect your account and personal data, we handle all transaction-related requests through our secure written channels."
* "We follow strict security and privacy policies to prevent unauthorized access to financial information. For any transaction-related inquiries, please contact us via [email/in app chat]."

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. *Why this approach?*
{panel}

* Financial data is considered *personal data* under GDPR, and discussing it over the phone without proper authentication creates *risks of unauthorized disclosure*.
* Unlike written channels, phone support *lacks robust identity verification*, increasing the risk of fraud.



If you need help choosing one of the 3 options I have given above, let me know; In any way, we can make sure that agents provide a *clear, professional, and security-focused response* without saying *"we're not allowed to"*, even without disclosing sensitive internal information 🙂

Apparently, there is no way to push changes to git automatically, so that should be done manually via Rundeck UI on a regular basis.

Also, this branch shouldn’t be changed externally (not via Rundeck UI) as it creates issues/conflicts as well.

hey [~accountid:712020:eb9cd4dd-46ca-47c8-a985-9f940495724a] 

* In such cases of analytics tools, the parties are usually considered joint controllers and leverage joint controllership agreement. However, as this applies some obligations to each party, big companies and some other parties conclude a C-2-C agreement with each party being responsible for their own processing activities.
* I agree that the points you highlighted re privacy notice disclosure is not something we usually commit to. 
** The statement re privacy notice may refer to two areas for us:
*** *Notice in the Restaurant app.* The way their Data Protection part is structured is that their services are usually integrated into the web and each user who interacts with the web - is a unique user (living individual). In our case, we will integrate it into the restaurant app and our users are a restaurant stuff, eg a unique ID will be assigned to the restaurant, not each stuff member. We do not and will not place any Privacy Notice in the restaurant app as the restaurant is not a living individual and there are no personal data, except users and some info about POC (rare cases). So this statement about the PN applies only when there is personal data involved and we may kindly ignore this obligation due to a low risk for us.
*** *Notice to courier/eater.* In this case, if we do not mask data, there is a data sharing with another controller (given the C-2-C relationship). *However, to eliminate the risk and make data anonymised for Clarity, we need to apply the masking level (see details below)*
* *Masking:* We need to push the team to apply the masking level that will hide all data about couriers/eaters: addresses, numbers, names, other info we can have about them in the order history.
** It can be a stronger level of masking than the loosest the team proposed.
** Let’s discuss with the team to mask all this data above to ensure (i) the risk to user’s /POC's data processing for unreasonable purposes is minimal and (ii) a burdensome PN requirement to us will not apply.
* *Using data, even restaurant's, for Microsoft own Ads:* we need to ask the team to push back on these clauses and turn off any usage of collected data for Microsoft’s advertising if this is possible. We can try and ask the team to check any settings during the integration, other details. If not possible, we need to mention to the team that restaurants can start receiving ads due to such a sharing and while it’s not personal data, some of the emails are still POC’s emails. 
* I agree that as this is the Restaurant app, the only personal data here is the data of couriers/eaters and rare cases - POC of the restaurants.
* All the in-app choices/movements by the Restaurant stuff cannot be considered personal data as the app is registered for a restaurant and we cannot identify, including Clarity, which specific user/person has been interacting with the app. The risk of personal data here is minimal.

Hi Lana,

# How should we proceed with cases where a refund is marked as successful, but the transaction details do not provide confirmation?

If refund is marked successfully from Beehive or Order page like [here|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/delivery-order/orders/212961947?cityId=1965], I would suggest to first check with #beehive-agent-support on Slack if there is any issue either with Beehive or Alfred. If that is not the case, they might ask you to create a ticket to Commerce Team, which is Food Customer Payments (here) to help check the issue. 

# Is there a way for us to retrieve proof of refund to verify whether the user actually received the funds?

Usually, if the refund is successfully completed, you will either see a green button icon with success for Bolt balance refund or a card icon with success for card refunds on this [page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%22248088872%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] next to the refund action. In this ticket case, if you check you can see that the partial refund action exist but there was no mention of a success or even the card icon is not shown. There is no documentation or official invoice that can be shared as proof of refund. In case the refund is successfully completed, you can either check the transaction history page for confirmation for Bolt balance refund or check the [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/2999506531] for card refund (there should be a status REFUNDED  on the payment page). After making sure the refund is successfully done, providing the user with the date the refund was made and the amount is enough for them to check the refund status with their bank. It is also necessary to educate the user that the refund process depends entirely on their bank and can take up to 10 (3o days maximum) for the amount to reflect back in their account.

# If manual refunds are indeed possible outside of Beehive, could you provide a step-by-step guide on how to process them?

Refunds are possible outside of beehive from the order page but I would not suggest to use them often, only in case of “urgency”. The accesses I previously shared are enough to be able to issue refund from the order page. In case of older orders refunds, accesses are restricted to some team leads because in the general processes, old orders refunds shouldn’t be provided to customers except some specific conditions are met. Theses accesses can be requested from [Admin|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/admin-access-request/access-requests/new] Administration>Access Requests>Raise Request and will need to be approved by an engineering manager and or team lead.

# In cases like this, where the refund process is unclear, should we escalate the issue to another team for verification?
This is already answered in point 1. Before escalation here, kindly check that the refund is not either sent to the Bolt balance or card by checking the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%22248088872%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] or the [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/2999506531]. If there is no mention of the refund and its status then it can be escalated to Food Customer Payments service desk.  


Coming back to this ticket, the issue here has been escalated to engineers and they are investigating the case. I am sorry my first reply was misleading as retrying the refund won’t work. As a workaround could you refund a different orders to the user’s card while we find a solution to fix this issue? There is currently no ETA for the fix.

*FEATURE ANALYSIS*

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Risk Profile = High*
{panel}

While the categories of data used in Blast Dispatch are not particularly sensitive, the nature of the processing (dispatching the same order to multiple drivers simultaneously) raises GDPR risks.

The following factors contribute to a higher-risk profile:

* The feature involves large-scale processing of geolocation data.
* The processing is highly automated and could significantly affect drivers' work conditions, including order allocation and potential earnings. (*arguable)*
* The decision-making process is algorithm-driven, potentially falling under *Article 22 (automated decision-making with significant effect).*
* Transparency concerns arise, particularly regarding how and why certain drivers receive offers while others do not.
* Worker organizations and regulators (ICO / AKI) are increasingly scrutinizing algorithmic management in ride-hailing, which could lead to regulatory inquiries.

Given these risks, *a DPIA will be necessary.*

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Personal data processed*
{panel}

{color:#ff5630}*_To be confirmed by the product team:_*{color}

*Driver data*:

# *Geolocation data* - Real-time location of drivers to determine proximity and availability for dispatch.
# *Order acceptance/rejection data* - details of whether a driver accepts or rejects a ride offer.
# *Historical order data* - Past ride completions, cancellations, and rejection trends (used for dispatch optimization).
# *Driver ID* - Unique identifiers to allocate and track dispatch decisions.
# *Availability status* - Whether a driver is currently available or engaged with another ride.
# *Order finish probability* - A calculated metric that predicts a driver’s likelihood of completing an order.

*Rider data*:

# *Order request details* - Time, location, and ride category.
# *Geolocation data* - Pickup and drop-off coordinates.
# *Ride acceptance time* - How long it takes for a driver to accept an offer.
# *Cancellation behavior* - Whether and when a rider cancels after a match is made.

*Data generated by algorithms -*{color:#ff5630} *_likely not personal data itself, but needs clarification on how we calculate this_*{color}

# *Order finish probability* – A predictive measure that estimates the likelihood of a ride being completed based on historical and real-time data.
# *Dispatch prioritization score* - Determines how many drivers receive the same ride offer.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Legal Basis*
{panel}

* The most appropriate legal basis appears to be *legitimate interest* (LI). However, this must be assessed via a Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA).
* The current driver privacy notice should be updated to explicitly mention legitimate interest as a legal basis.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Article 22 – Automated Decision-Making*
{panel}

* Blast Dispatch operates through *solely automated decision-making*.
* The core question is whether it has a *significant effect* on drivers. Given that the allocation of orders directly impacts driver earnings, it could be argued that it does.
* If caught under Article 22, relying on *consent or human review* would be impractical. Therefore, we must build a justification that the decision does not have a significant impact or that it falls within an exemption under Article 22(2).

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Transparency*
{panel}

* There is a *high risk of drivers not understanding why they receive certain order offers and not others*.
* To mitigate this, transparency measures should include:
** A clear explanation in the driver app UI.
** Updates to the driver privacy notice to explicitly describe how the dispatch system works.
** Internal documentation to justify the algorithm’s fairness and non-discriminatory nature.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Back-end processing / DSARs*
{panel}

* The system must ensure that drivers can *access relevant data* when submitting a *Data Subject Access Request (DSAR)*.
* This includes:
** A record of order offers received, rejected, and accepted.
** Information on how dispatch decisions were made (without exposing proprietary algorithm details).

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Overlap with regulatory scrutiny*
{panel}

* The *ICO and AKI* are likely to scrutinize automated driver allocation.
* Responses to regulator inquiries should emphasize fairness, non-discrimination, and efficiency benefits.
* We must document how each data category factors into dispatch decisions to justify compliance.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Next steps*
{panel}

*Privacy Actions:*

* Conduct a *DPIA* to assess risks in detail.
* Conduct a *LIA* to justify reliance on legitimate interest.
* Update the *driver privacy notice* to reflect this processing activity.
* Ensure that DSAR responses include relevant order allocation details. - *if decided that it’s required*

*Stakeholder Actions:*

* *Most important -* stakeholders need to *review and confirm the personal data processed.* Especially regarding *how we calculate the the order finish probability.*
* Inform stakeholders that *drivers will be aware* of the dispatch method via DSARs and potential regulator inquiries.
* Clarify how *dispatch decisions will be explained to drivers* - will there be guidance materials or in-app explanations?
* Confirm whether drivers will have a *means to challenge dispatch decisions*.

Thanks [~accountid:60528926695c3900706cc79e] - I include my thoughts below.

+*General Observations*+

* I am hesitant to create 'template responses' here without seeing the _specific_ questions that we are seeing from UK councils. As such, please take the below as general guidance rather than word-for-word responses that we should be sharing externally. Ultimately, if a UK council sends us a question with Privacy relevance, you should loop in our team to help with answering that specific question.
* The below guidance primarily concerns _personal data_. If you are looking for answers on all data that Bolt handles and stores, you will also need to link up with Ops.

+*Guidance on Questions*+

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# *Is data actually stored in the office or the cloud?*
{panel}

* Regarding what physical paper records Bolt stores in its UK offices, this is a question for UK Ops (i.e., Jason Camilleri and his team).
** I am aware that we collect some data from drivers/riders on paper in the London Driver Hub where we are dealing with lost item cases. However,Ops would be better placed to provide a more comprehensive list of examples.
* However, it is reasonable to assume that we store the majority of our data electronically, rather than as physical copies in the Bolt offices.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# *Where is the data stored and by whom?*
{panel}

* The Privacy Team are currently conducting a mapping exercise regarding which Bolt entities process and store personal data regarding UK users. This is currently ongoing, and I will provide you with an update as soon as I hear back on this.
**  The relevant entities are likely to be a combination of Bolt UK Services Limited (UK), Bolt Technology OU (Estonia) and Bolt Operations OU (Estonia). But as I say, this is TBC.
* However, I can confirm the following for now:
** Bolt’s main servers are located in Frankfurt (Germany).
** Where HQ tools are involved (e.g., Admin / Beehive), data is processed and accessed globally (rather than locally on a per-office basis).
** Where Bolt uses other third-party tools (e.g., Google Drive, Slack), the data collected via these tools is originally processed locally (i.e., the country where the employees / users are based) and is subsequently stored wherever those third parties' servers are located.
** Our preference when using third-party tools is to either: (1) store data in the EU; or (2) store data in a country that has been deemed ‘adequate’ by the European Commission.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# *How is it compliant to store data in the cloud?*
{panel}

* Yes it is, provided the following steps are taken (which to be clear, Bolt has taken):
** We choose compliant third-party providers and have entered into appropriate data protection agreements with them (e.g., we have data processing agreements with Box and Google).
** We ensure data is encrypted at rest and in transit to protect it from unauthorised access (Bolt does this).
** We carefully consider where the data is stored to ensure that it is secure (as mentioned above, our preference  is to either: (1) store data in the EU; or (2) store data in a country that has been deemed ‘adequate’ by the European Commission).
** We ensure that strict access controls are in place to control who can access any data on the cloud, and from where.

We can have multiple tiers denoted in yml files, but the main thing is what to still run if shit hits the fan and how can we prepare for these things in advance with relatively low effort.

It would be great if we can mark dbt models that materialise as incremental or table with a priority mark. This can be a meta tier config, but could also just be a tag. Then during major outages, platform should be able to turn on a setting ‘urgent only’ and run databricks workflows that run only the critical models. All other pipelines could get blocked. We can have one of those workflows per project that would only run when data platform triggers it.

We can once in a while do stress testing where data platform can tell us that the run time needs to decrease if we have marked too many models or they take too long.

On my side if I would have three intermediate models - A, B, C - feeding into a critical mart called D (e.g. business review) but only one (model A) of delivers super critical metrics, then I can run a pipeline on a tag that or tier that only runs A and D. It will be fast, have data for what matters, and the business can continue while we buy ourselves time to pick up the pieces.

+*LIST OF QUESTIONS / FLAGS FOR STAKEHOLDERS*+ (DC-specific)

*(1) General information on the feature*

* Are any third parties involved in implementing the feature (e.g., running the model, collecting the data, subsequent recipients of the data to review it etc.)? If so, do we already have agreements in place with them?
* Are any IT tools / applications / platforms used as part of this feature?
* Which Bolt entities will be collecting and processing this data? Will this be purely a local Bolt entity (e.g., Bolt UK Services Limited), Bolt Technology OU or Bolt Operations OU?
* I assume the feature does not involve the use of Payment Card Industry Data Security Standards?
* Has a process flow (re the data being collected and used for the feature) been prepared?
* What types of security measures are in place for this project? Also, who will have access to the dataflows?
* Do you consider that the proposal is in line with Bolt’s Information Security Policies and Guidelines, especially the Information Security Policy, the Access Control Policy, the Data Encryption Policy, and the Data Backup Policy? Has the InfoSec team reviewed it?
* Where will the data be stored (i.e., inside the UK / EU, or in another country)?
* How long do we intend to store this data for?

*(2) Info on the algorithm*

* Are all 50 categories of data used to evaluate order try elasticity (as set out on the Confluence page) strictly necessary for making this evaluation? Can any be stripped out?

*(3) Transparency*

* Will we be publishing guidance materials for drivers that explain how Dynamic Commission works?
* Will the driver be able to clearly see in the app / through UI that a trip is subject to Dynamic Commission?
* What information about the categories of data used here / the decisions made are we comfortable with sharing with drivers that request such information as part of a data subject access request?
* Are we comfortable with the details of processing / the algorithm potentially becoming public? This information may be subject to disclosure as a result of the ICO investigation (as well as any other investigation by regulators).
* If challenged, could we comfortably argue that use of models like this is standard market practice?

*(4) Challenging decisions*

* I am aware that we have a process for drivers challenging journey fees in the UK. Will drivers similarly be able to challenge a journey fee calculated on the basis of Dynamic Commission? If so, how?
* If a driver objected to using the data to calculate Dynamic Commission, operationally would we be able to cease processing for individual drivers?

*(5) Reclass risk*

* Was Product legal consulted about reclass risk here, given that we are arguably nudging drivers to accept a trip?

In short, this is a WIE request relating to the suspension of a UK driver’s account. Background is below.

*BACKGROUND*

* On 4 September, a UK driver was asked to complete selfie verification. When doing so, our systems picked up significant changes in their geo-positioning when they did so.
** In particular, the selfie verification process started in London. The selfie upload was finalised from a different device in Bristol. This suggested that someone else may have access to the account.
* On the same day, access to the account was restricted and the incident was reported to TfL. The driver was given 30 days to appeal and provide evidence.
* On 5 September, the driver wrote to Bolt with the following explanation:
** “_Recently, I traveled to Uganda for a family meeting and returned on Monday. Upon my return, I received an email from Bolt requesting that I send a picture of my updated plastic front driver’s license, which I did on Tuesday. I was waiting for Bolt to reactivate my account. Yesterday morning, I was in Bristol and received an email from Bolt informing me that my account had been updated and that I should sign in. Unfortunately, I did not have my work phone with me in Bristol, so I downloaded the Bolt app on a new device to check if my account was active and see if I could go online in Bristol. During the login process, I was asked to take a selfie for verification, which usually works. However, this time, I received a message stating that my account was suspended for fraudulent activity._”
** It appears that this explanation was not sufficient evidence for the Safety and Compliance Team, who then decided to permanently suspend the account.
* It appears that in early October, the driver visit the London hub to provide a photo of their ID and a new profile photo. It is not clear why this did not resolve the matter.

* *There is no other legal basis besides consent* - as biometric data for the purpose of identification falls under special category of personal data (Article 9(2)(a) GDPR). 
** While the current consent form (which was recently updated) could be updated again instead of asking consent in a separate pop-up notification, it has to be made entirely clear that this consent also applies to the *processing* and *storing* the biometric data for this exact purpose.
** In the current DPIA, it is stated that asking for consent is not planned for this feature as it would create a loophole for the fraudsters, which would defeat the purpose of the database. *Without explicit consent, this processing will not be lawful under GDPR.*
* There are some remaining questions:
** *How will we ensure that the biometrics (either stored in AWS or internally) are properly encrypted/other measures are taken to ensure the data is safe?* In the event of a data incident, the storage of biometrics poses a heightened risk of extreme harm - compromise of such sensitive data can lead to severe consequences for users. Unlike other forms of personal data, biometrics are inherently linked to user’s identity, which makes it extremely valuable to scammers + it increases the potential of long-lasting risk to the individuals, even when the data incident itself has been solved. 
** *Taken from the DPIA: “The data is stored inside the EU only. It never leaves the EU. RuralShores + IronMountain agents are located in India and they process the data remotely from there, but the data is never ever stored in a location outside of the EU.” -* we need a better explanation on how this will look like. Which systems are RuralShores + IronMountain agents using then, as they are located in India? Does this mean that even e.g. the logs of processing the biometrics will not be stored in India? 
** *Under “How did you get the data”, it says 1. Directly from an individual by Bolt and 2 Reuse of data* - as we need to rely on consent as the legal basis, we cannot reuse the data that we have previously collected. 
** *How do we make sure we will catch only fraudsters with this processing?* Will there be a human review of the flagged users? We need to make sure we don’t create harm for innocent users with this. 
*** What will be the process when the user appeals the decision? Will it be our CS agents reviewing it?

Regarding your question about minors providing delivery services, there is no legislation in the Czech Republic specifically aimed at underage couriers. Employment of minors is generally covered by the Labour Code, which sets out, among other things, the conditions of employment of minors. *It is forbidden to employ minors under the age of 15 or minors who have not completed compulsory schooling* (this is regulated, in addition to the Labour Code, by the Civil Code and the Employment Act).

Other restrictions regarding the employment of minors according to the Labour Code include:

* The maximum working time shall be 40 hours per week and shall not exceed 8 hours in any one day. There must be a break of at least 12 hours between shifts. Minors must be given a break after four and a half hours of work
* Minors cannot work overtime.
* Minors cannot work in the night.
* There are also types of work that minors cannot do because they would be at increased risk of injury or endangering others. Examples include work involving the handling of loads, the manufacture and processing of explosives, work performed at an imposed pace, work performed in confined spaces or tanks, slaughtering animals in slaughterhouses, etc.
* Regarding the salary, the only restriction of salaries of minors is the minimum wage set by the government.

_Thank you for reaching out regarding the smoke detection results from your recent vehicle rental. We understand your concerns and would like to clarify how our detection system operates._

Rather than providing a single-point reading, they establish a baseline of neutral air quality and detect any significant deviations from that baseline. In this case, the recorded data indicates a clear spike in smoke concentration over a period of seven minutes, followed by fluctuations typical of airborne particulate dispersal._

_Given this methodology, the results are based on a consistent pattern of air quality changes over time, rather than an isolated reading. This approach provides a reliable indication of smoking activity within the vehicle._

* *Consent:* The updated consent form could be revised instead of introducing a separate pop-up, but it must be crystal clear about biometric data usage.
* *Data Security:* We need to outline the encryption and protection measures for biometric data stored in AWS or internally, considering the heightened risks in case of a data breach.
* *Remote Processing:* Further clarification is needed on how RuralShores and IronMountain agents (based in India) access the data remotely, ensuring no storage or logs exist outside the EU.
* *Fraud Detection & Appeals:* We need to confirm if human review will be involved in assessing flagged users and define the appeal process (e.g., CS agent involvement).
* *Account Deletion:* Confirmation is needed on whether biometric data is deleted when a user deletes their account.
* *Reuse of Data:* Since consent is the legal basis, we cannot reuse previously collected data - this needs to be reflected in our approach.

ODPO engaged NJORD to undertake a legal review of the DPIA to see whether we could mitigate the overall risk and avoid consultation with the regulator.

{noformat}SELECT 
    etl.created_date AS order_date, 
    APPROX_DISTINCT(etl.order_id) AS approx_order_count
FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders AS etl
LEFT JOIN ng_public.fraud_order_check AS foc 
    ON etl.order_id = foc.order_id 
    AND etl.city_id = foc.city_id 
    AND foc.created_date BETWEEN DATE '2025-01-01' AND DATE '2025-01-30'
LEFT JOIN ng_public.fraud_order_check_result AS focr 
    ON focr.order_check_id = foc.id
    AND focr.created_date BETWEEN DATE '2025-01-01' AND DATE '2025-01-30'
LEFT JOIN ng_public.company_order AS co 
    ON co.id = etl.order_id 
    AND co.city_id = etl.city_id 
    AND co.created_date BETWEEN DATE '2025-01-01' AND DATE '2025-01-30'
JOIN ng_public.company_order_destination AS cod 
    ON co.id = cod.order_id 
    AND co.city_id = cod.city_id 
    AND cod.created_date BETWEEN DATE '2025-01-01' AND DATE '2025-01-30'
WHERE etl.country_code = 'ae'
AND etl.created_date BETWEEN DATE '2025-01-01' AND DATE '2025-01-30'
AND ROUND(great_circle_distance(co.real_destination_lat, co.real_destination_lng, 
                                cod.destination_lat, cod.destination_lng), 2) >= 5 
AND focr."type" = 'RIDE_DID_NOT_HAPPEN'
GROUP BY etl.created_date
ORDER BY etl.created_date DESC{noformat}

To handle the first 2 items reported by Maciej we need to reindex the cluster with new index settings because we cannot dynamically change the settings of the current index. What this means? We need to create a new index with the new settings and the old data will be copied to the new index applying the new partitioning and the ‘new’ filter.

There are 3 things that we need to know:

# During this process the write alias of the current index will point to the new index so the backend services won’t see the new data written to the new index since the read alias is pointing to the ‘old’ data. We discussed we the team and we are ok with this partial unavailability during the reindex process.
# We will use this script from the tools repo to do the reindexing: [https://github.com/bolteu/tools/tree/master/geo/elasticsearch_reindex|https://github.com/bolteu/tools/tree/master/geo/elasticsearch_reindex|smart-link] 
# The estimated duration of the reindexing is at most 5h. How do we know that? geo-core team has done this recently and for a 1.1TB index their reindex process took [34h|https://monitor.boltint.net/d/000000015/elastic3a-cluster?orgId=1&var-server=P8814D9327E90C53F&var-cluster=locations-orders-live&var-log_level=All&var-filename=All&from=1737534156115&to=1737686041257] throttling the process to 20k documents/s([requests_per_second|https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/docs-reindex.html#docs-reindex-throttle])

The plan:

# Play locally with the scripts to make sure everything is ok. Meanwhile make a list of useful queries to monitor the process. Will put the list here.
# Test the changes in prelive
# Wait for SRE to decrease disk usage in live to at most 40%
# Run the script in live early in the morning(6.30AM EEST) so we don’t overlap with peak hours and also to be able to monitor the entire process and react to any issues that might appear.

We received a legal opinion on dashcams in Washington DC. It concludes that there are no specific U.S. federal or District of Columbia laws prohibiting the use of dashboard cameras without audio on e-scooters for recording accidents or thefts. However, it provides key recommendations to ensure compliance with general privacy and consumer protection laws:

# *Notice & Transparency* - Scooters should have clear and conspicuous notices informing users that video recording is taking place for safety and security purposes. Any additional uses (e.g., AI training) should be disclosed.
# *No Audio Recording* - Audio recording should be disabled to avoid triggering wiretapping laws, which impose significant legal risks.
# *Privacy Policy Updates* - Bolt should update its privacy notice to cover video recording, treating it as personal data and disclosing potential sharing (e.g., with law enforcement or insurers).
# *Consent for Unexpected Uses* - If recordings will be used in ways users may not anticipate, additional consent should be obtained via the mobile app or onboarding process.
# *Access Restrictions* - Access to recordings should be limited to necessary personnel, following FTC enforcement principles on data security.
# *Data Retention* - There is no specific requirement related to the retention of dashcam footage, nor is there a specific requirement to disclose Bolt’s data retention practices under current federal or DC law.

Dear Volodymyr,

We write further to your recent data subject rights request, which we received on 3 November 2024. Thank you for your patience. We include our response below.

*(1) Data sharing with Meta*

Bolt engages with third-party analytics providers such as Appsflyer, which can result in sharing certain user information between Bolt and Meta for marketing and analytics purposes. The extent of such sharing depends on the tracking permissions that a user has enabled in the Bolt app.

When a user installs or opens the Bolt app for the first time after downloading it from the App Store, the user is asked whether they wish to opt-in to the App Tracking Transparency (“*ATT*”) framework in the form of a prompt (“_Allow Bolt: Request a Ride to track your activity across other companies' apps and websites?_”).

* If the user selects “_Allow_”, this grants permission for Bolt to track the user’s activity across certain apps and websites. As a result, Bolt may share certain user information such as the user’s identifier for advertisers (“*IDFA*”), device information and hashed contact information with Meta.
* If the user selects “_Ask App Not to Track_”, then Bolt will not share the above with Meta. However, Bolt may still share a user’s events data and aggregated postbacks.

You can find further information on how Bolt processes your personal data in our privacy notice available at [https://bolt.eu/pl-pl/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/pl-pl/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides] . Please note in particular the following section:

* “*_Partnerzy promocyjni, marketingowi i strategiczni:_* _Możemy udostępniać ograniczone dane – np. Państwa adres e-mail – partnerom promocyjnym, marketingowym i strategicznym, aby mogli informować Państwa o wydarzeniach promocyjnych oraz przekazywać Państwu informacje i wiadomości marketingowe dotyczące produktów lub usług, które mogą Państwa zainteresować. Ponadto możemy udostępniać Państwa dane osobowe dostawcom platform marketingowych, w tym reklamodawcom aktywnym w mediach społecznościowych, sieciom reklamowym i zewnętrznym dostawcom danych. Chodzi o to, aby docierać do Pasażerów, lepiej ich poznać, mierzyć skuteczność naszych reklam na innych platformach oraz w serwisach społecznościowych takich jak Facebook czy Google_.”

*(2) Opting-out*

You can change your tracking permissions at any time by taking the following steps in the Bolt app:

# Go to *Settings* > *Privacy & security* > *Tracking*.
# Toggle ‘off’ tracking for any apps where you do not want those apps to track your activity across other apps and websites.

You can also remove Bolt’s permissions regarding activity tracking by logging into your Facebook account and going to *Settings & privacy* > *Your activity and permissions > Apps and websites*.

*(3) Your rights*

You have the right to request rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing of personal data concerning you or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You have the right to complain directly to the appropriate supervisory authority and seek a judicial remedy. 

If you have any additional questions, please let us know.

Yours sincerely,

*Bolt*

To sum up, Emplifi is being phased out as HQ transitions to Sprout starting January 31. Due to pricing considerations, our market has decided to use a different platform ContentStudio for social media management.

ContentStudio offers the same functionalities as Emplifi, enabling us to monitor, manage, and analyze social media activities. It allows us to respond to messages on Bolt Georgia’s Facebook and Instagram pages, monitor and reply to comments, and track company mentions in posts and stories. Additionally, it includes market analysis tools that meet the marketing team’s needs. The only limitation we have identified is that it does not integrate with Looker.

To proceed, we need HQ’s (your) approval to register an account for Bolt Georgia’s Facebook and Instagram on ContentStudio. We also need to determine the payment procedure whether HQ will handle the registration and provide access and invoices, or if we can complete these steps independently.

From a legal perspective, there are no specific laws in Georgia that directly regulate social network operations, meaning there are no legal restrictions on selecting this platform. However, we are ensuring compliance with privacy regulations, and ContentStudio’s privacy policy is detailed in its terms and conditions, which we can share for your review. - [here|https://contentstudio.io/privacy-policy] 

Additionally, when we previously used Emplifi, no additional records or formal approvals were required. Given this precedent, we believe the transition from Emplifi to ContentStudio should be straightforward. However, as February approaches, we would like to finalize this change promptly to avoid unnecessary costs related to Emplifi.

I would also like to point out that the selection process was not easy. Please don't think that we simply chose ContentStudio without consideration. We are sharing with you the list of priorities that guided our decision.

After giving this more thought, I’ve identified some issues.

Using the charger to wake up the battery is fine and should work.

However, the problem arises when trying to use IoT to wake up the battery. During upfitting, IoT is turned off and only wakes up when it receives 24V from the ECU. This means IoT cannot be the one to wake up the BMS. Additionally, the IoT backup battery does not wake up IoT.

Hello Miglė, 

Thank you for your request. 

We don’t have a list of articles that require escalation. The global rules are applied, as generally stated at the top of the article 🌍 [Escalation guidelines|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/4407518583058] (this is the only article on escalation workflow we currently have). If they differ by market, this should be noted in the “Market-specific escalations guidelines” section. 

The processes are not linked to this section due to the following reasons: 

* Escalations after the first reply just need an internal note added, and the Tier changed. Those processes would be really short. 
* The cases that are supposed to be escalated after some completed steps have more general descriptions. For example, any blocking case can fall under various issue types and, therefore, articles. The list would be very long and hard to keep up to date. 

We also don’t reference the Escalation guidelines in any articles. Since the market-specific rules vary heavily, we rely on agents to know the rules for their country and keep the possible escalation in mind. 

Moreover, when a case is escalated, agents are expected to leave an internal note with an overview of why they did so. This can either happen based on market-specific guidelines or a stand-alone process. In both cases, the relevant KB article should be linked in the internal note. This is stated in the Escalation guidelines, as well as  🌍 [Guidelines for leaving comments and internal notes|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/6615970744978]. 

I believe that a conducted deep-dive would effectively uncover what escalations are based upon in Lithuania. If the cases don’t have the reason listed, it’s either an incorrect escalation or missing info in the internal note. Those possible issues would be the best to address with your local Quality reviewer. 

We generally rely on the markets to notify us about changes in their escalation process. So, if you find any cases that should be added/removed from the list, please let us know, and we’ll update them. 

Thank you, and have a nice Friday! ✨

----

Dear Damir,

Thank you for your data subject rights request, which we received on 21 January 2025.

We take your privacy seriously. As a part of this commitment, we would like to clarify Bolt’s practices in relation to collecting and processing your location information.

Bolt may use your geolocation data for various purposes, including to suggest new rides and destinations depending on the consents you have provided in your Bolt app. You can always disable these specific notifications, without disabling all Bolt notifications. Further information in this regard can be found in our privacy notice available at [https://bolt.eu/en-mt/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/en-mt/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides]  .

Additionally, please note the following:

* Bolt starts collecting your location data when you grant permission to tracking it for either ‘All time', ‘While using the App’ or ‘Once’. Bolt asks for such permission on sign-in; however, such permission can be revoked or granted at any time via your device settings (either when a prompt to authorise background use is displayed in the Bolt app or on your own). Your location information is collected only in the foreground. This means that Bolt starts collecting your location data when you open the Bolt app and stops collecting it when you close the Bolt app.
* The permission to share your location data ‘All the time’ applies only to the geofencing feature, which is used to notify you if Bolt is operating in a specific geographic area. Bolt does not, however, store any of your location data in relation to this. iOS and Android devices enable apps to automatically trigger notifications when the user enters a specific geographic area. This does not require the Bolt app to run in the background or mobile data to be used. Apple and Android store this information at their end and automatically trigger those notifications when a user enters a defined geographic area, without sharing the user’s location with Bolt.

*Your rights* 

You have the right to request rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing of personal data concerning you or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You have the right to complain directly to the appropriate supervisory authority and seek a judicial remedy. 

If you have any additional questions, please let us know.

Yours sincerely,

*Bolt*

Hi [~accountid:712020:8c797c70-7a57-496e-aa3f-5d91df806eb2] - I have taken a look at the below and unfortunately I am still confused as to the rationale being applied here. I think this is the result of communication:

* As I mentioned before, if we intend to take any of the applicants beyond the recruitment stage, then we will need to have some privacy notice language in place that covers them anyway. If we do not want to mention Modash / some of the drafting I have suggested in the the privacy notice annex, *it sounds like what you are asking for is two separate privacy notices* - one that covers the recruitment process, and another that covers that the applicants that enter into contracts with Bolt - is that right?
* If this is right, then *this is not standard practice and would create extra unnecessary effort* - privacy notices are typically designed to cover lots of different processing scenarios, and the privacy notice language contained in [this doc|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Qd5AMI3PoQJV0Y8J52H_lujEfselU0nXNLldiUOI8gI/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.gjdgxs] could cover both: (a) unsuccessful applicants and (b) successful applicants.
* *Including data protection terms in an agreement that regulate data processing is a separate issue to having a privacy notice in place*. The former is a set of contractual provisions that the individual will agree to, whereas the latter is a general information document in which individuals can find information about the processing of their personal data by Bolt. The reason this distinction is important is because: (1) we need a privacy notice for both unsuccessful applicants +*and*+ applicants that sign an agreement with us; and (2) we +*only*+ need data protection terms for applicants that sign an agreement with us.

I have therefore marked-up the privacy notice language to cover both unsuccessful and successful applicants ([~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e] if you have some time next week, would you also mind taking a [look|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Qd5AMI3PoQJV0Y8J52H_lujEfselU0nXNLldiUOI8gI/edit?tab=t.0] for good measure?) . Hi team, 

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount. 


Please let me know if you have any other questions.

Cheers,
Afiba

I see two realistic outcomes:

* Method 1 - We *keep sending batteries in scooters as is - connected to controllers and hatches closed*
** We must keep them in *transportation mode* (new FW) to be *waken up by charging the scooter directly* to avoid ECU draining the battery.
** We need to drag the charger to every single charger one-by-one and use the custom hatch unlock IOT to access the batteries and remove them.
* Method 2 - We *change the packing method* to *isolate battery connectors safely* and wrap/strap the hatches in order to not lock the batteries inside scooters.
** We would not have to change the FW, which means we do not have to “activate” the battery, nor open the hatch with customized tooling.

In my opinion, the second method is more preferred, as then LOPS does not have to waste time carrying around a charger to “activate” batteries and open hatches with a custom IOT tool (which they lose & break easily from experience). It is easier if they can just remove the hatches and batteries physically during the unpacking without any special tools or other wizardry, and insert when upfitting is done having either charged or not (depending on the process of testing vehicles).

{quote}However, the problem arises when trying to use IoT to wake up the battery. During upfitting, IoT is turned off and only wakes up when it receives 24V from the ECU. This means IoT cannot be the one to wake up the BMS. Additionally, the IoT backup battery does not wake up IoT.{quote}

*UPD:* 

*Problem statement:* 

The Kenya Data Protection Act obliges that "The data controller or data processor shall consult the ODPC prior to the processing if a data protection impact assessment prepared under this section indicates that the processing of the data would result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of a data subject."

*Questions to answer:*

* Does this mean that for certain processing activities that are automatically deemed as high risk (Article 41 (1) of the Data Protection Regulations [here|https://www.odpc.go.ke/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/THE-DATA-PROTECTION-GENERAL-REGULATIONS-2021-1.pdf]), *both* the DPIA and consultation are required automatically?
* Or does it mean that a DPIA for such processing activities is *always* required, but the consultation is required *only if* a prepared DPIA indicates *a high risk*? If the risk in the DPIA has been mitigated to "medium" or "low," is the consultation not required?


*ODPO team’s advice:* 
* Based on the review of the following reference materials:

* The Regulatory Framework
** The Data Protection Act - Article 31
** The Data Protection Regulations - Article 49-51
** The ODPC Guidance on DPIA
* The Audio - Trip Audi Recording DPIA
* The note prepared by the Privacy Counsel (screenshots above),

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
I agree with the conclusion made by the Privacy Counsel that *we do not have to consult with ODPC* regarding the DPIA conducted for the Audio-Trip-Recording feature.
{panel}

*My conclusion is based on my understanding/interpretation of Article 31 (3) of the Data Protection Act*: If you're a data controller or processor in Kenya, and you conduct a DPIA for a planned data processing activity, and that DPIA shows that this activity could seriously harm the privacy rights of the people whose data you're handling (i.e. DPIA comes back as “high risk“), then you must consult to the Data Commissioner before you start that processing. Since in our case the DPIA risk has been lowered to *"medium"* after implementing the suggested measures, we don't have to consult with the ODPC.
